newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Fertiliser to grow AECI year shr.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Fertiliser to grow AECI year shr.

text.p: Better agricultural conditions last year are expected to boost South African chemicals group AECI Ltd's earnings for the year to end-December 1996, analysts said on Friday.
They said good rains during the first half of 1996 had allowed most farmers to spend cash on crop fertilisers, the main product of AECI's operating company Kynoch Ltd.
"Their earnings should be slightly up, not a great deal," said one analyst, who did not want to be named.
"Things like fertilisers have been selling very well. The farmers had quite a reasonable crop last year...(and) a bit of money to spend on fertilisers...," he added.
Analysts polled by Reuters predict earnings per share on a range of 277 to 280 cents, up from 255 cents, when AECI reports its results on Tuesday. The consensus figure was 278.2 cents.
The dividend is seen between 85 and 92.5 cents a share, up from 83 cents. Consensus was at 89.2 cents.

"Fertiliser prices have kind of bounced along the $200 resistance level...They are up now to about $220 a ton. Kynoch (a unit of AECI) has done particularly well...especially seeing that the maize and sugar industries had a particularly good year with good rains," another analyst said.
Themis Themistocleous, an oils and chemicals analyst at stockbroker SBC Warburg, said Kynoch was likely to contribute about 23 percent to the group's overall earnings for 1996.
"The fertiliser business will be the main driver of their earnings," one analyst commented.

Themistocleous said a weaker rand had spurred exports by AECI's explosives, chemicals and fertiliser operating companies. But he added low international polyester and polymer prices could dull profits at the group's South African Nylon Spinners (SANS) unit and Polifin -- the plastics and chemicals operation. "So with a weaker rand they did not get the full benefits because the international markets were weak," he said.

One analyst who declined to be named said the continued influx of illegal textiles into the country had likely affected SANS's earnings potential from the domestic market last year. Analysts expect no major drive in earnings from AECI's one-year-old KwaZulu-Natal lysin animal feed plant -- a joint-venture with the state's Industrial Development Corp. They said the 250 million rand plant had operated below capacity.
"The lysin project...is running below capacity at this stage and they are building up towards full capacity, but it is still no where close to that," Themistocleous said.
Analysts said AECI could expect a slightly better 1997 with international fertiliser prices looking set to firm.

Good rains, which have fallen in most parts of the country in the past few weeks, and higher chemical prices were seen a driving force for a mild upward swing in AECI's earnings for the first half of 1997.
Themistocleous added: "I think 1997 is going to be a good year...a lot of growth will come through Polifin mainly because of chemical prices.
